But as they were going back to the camp, one of the men touched the side of the canoe again, and they both fell down once more. And when they awoke in the morning, they were back at the head of the river, back at the strange village.

This happened three times, and each time Gwezo and his men brought presents to the village of the spirit, until finally the spirit let them take the two men back to the camp for good.

The answer is: ...came to visit him [Johnny]... [they] were John Oro Cob and William Waswasesicamod. They walked in, and sitting down, smoking their pipes, began to laugh. Johnny asked them what was so funny? They replied, "What is there to joke about?" When he persisted, they told him. "There is no use talking to Johnny," said they. "We have told him often enough." What had they noted about Johnny? He had a sore finger. While he was sitting there thinking, two big raccoons came along. Without a moment's hesitation, Johnny reached for his rifle and, with a couple of well-aimed shots, stopped them both. "You see. . ." said John Oro Cob, "you have never been good for much, Johnny, except to show off your rifle."

This story, with variations, has been reported from several Midwestern Native American communities, including the Ojibwa and the Ho-Chunk. Similar stories are also found in other Native American and Native Canadian cultures. Despite the similarities, it is unlikely that a single progenitor story exists, since the underlying message of the tale can vary considerably depending on the community and the teller. Some versions of the story are told as a cautionary tale about the dangers of laughter. In this version, it is the two friends who are punished for their lack of respect for Johnny. According to Bryant (1999), among the Eastern Band of Cherokees, the story is told to emphasize the importance of respect for all creatures, even those who may seem insignificant or unimportant.

They drank the water, and they quenched their thirst. But as they drank, they saw their faces in the water, and they saw that their faces were not the faces of men. They were the faces of bears.

Explanation
This is a story from the Ojibwe people. It is a cautionary tale, a warning about the dangers of alcohol. The two men had been out hunting, and they had been drinking. When they looked into the water, they saw their true natures. They were no longer men; they were bears.

Variants
There are many variants of this story, but they all follow the same pattern. A man or a group of men go out hunting, they drink too much alcohol, and then they lose their humanity. Sometimes the men turn into wolves; sometimes they turn into bears; sometimes they turn into something else altogether. But the message is always the same: alcohol is a dangerous thing, and it can turn you into something other than a human being.

Origins
This story may have originated among the Ojibwe people. The Ojibwe are a First Nations group who live in Canada and the United States. They are also known as the Chippewa. The Ojibwe people have many stories about the dangers of alcohol. One story tells how alcohol was introduced into the world. A man was tasked with looking after the sacred fire. He was forbidden to touch the fire. But he was curious, and he touched the fire with his feet. The fire burned him, and he cried out in pain. The people came running, and they saw that their friend was no longer a man; he had become a frog.

They went out to Pound Lake, and as they approached the water's edge, they saw a great many whitefish rising to the surface. "This is a good sign," said the men. "We shall have a bounty of fish." 
They cast their nets and soon had more fish than they could carry. They returned to the village with their nets full. "See how well our dreams have come true," said one man to another. "We have enough fish for ourselves and our friends."

The legend of the Dream Fisher
In the legend of the Dream Fisher, recorded among the Tsimshian and cited by W.H.Bridge in his 1851 book The Indian Tribes of British Columbia, the dream represents the vitality and interconnectedness of all life. The dream is not simply a personal vision, but a prophecy that is fulfilled when the dreamer takes action on the basis of the dream. The dreamer does not enjoy the bounty of the fish alone, but shares the catch with his friends and relatives.

But when they came out of the cave the next morning, someone had taken their clothes.Under Canadian law at the time, the sexual act itself was not illegal, but the absence of clothes made the act of buggery. The two men were arrested and charged.

In R. v. Easter, Fred Easter and John Campbell were convicted of the offence of buggery. On appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, the conviction was overturned. The justices ruling was that the lack of a "normal" intent element in the section covering buggery was unconstitutional. The court ruled that "the mere fact that some embarrassment or insult may attend the questioning of an individual as to his sexual preferences or practices does not make the question insulting or inconsistent with human dignity."

There is a memorial plaque to the men of Easter Cove, referring to this case. It was placed there in 1991, eleven years after the verdict, by the Canadian Society for International Law.

Ecology
Pound Ridge is an area of woodland surrounding a large rock outcrop. It is the home of a number of animal species typical of the northern Appalachian Mountains. Some of the animals seen in the area include the bobcat, coyote, black bear, and the occasional gray wolf. There is also a significant population of rattlesnakes. The area is also noted for its bird life, with over 150 species recorded. A combination of factors including forest management practices, the proximity of open areas, and a somewhat dry climate combine to make Pound Ridge an Ideal habitat for birds. Many species that are at risk or endangered elsewhere in New York State, such as the eastern bluebird and the northern red-legged frog, can be found at Pound Ridge.Oliver Cromwell Pitts, a Yale University trained Ecologist and Naturalist visited Pound Ridge in 1937.  He would return on and off over the next thirty years. Perhaps they knew that the growing number of white settlers posed a threat to their own way of life, or perhaps they were merely fearful of the reprisals that would surely follow any attack on the New Osnaburg settlement.  Whatever the reason, their arrival would soon turn to disaster.

The Ktunaxa people are one of the First Nations of Canada. Their traditional territory is the inland caribou region of the north Rocky Mountains, covering approximately 180,000 square kilometers (70,000 sq mi) between the Rocky Mountains and the Purcell and Selkirk mountains. The Ktunaxa people were the most numerous of the pre-Contact Native populations of British Columbia. Before the arrival of Europeans, the population is estimated to have been between 12,000 and 15,000 people living in 150 to 180 villages. After the arrival of Europeans, the population declined rapidly due to diseases brought by fur trade contacts and concentrating in a smaller number of villages. The Ktunaxa people are characterized by their long history of intertribal trade and marriage relationships, extending as far as the Great Plains to the east.Their history is marked by three distinct eras: the pre-Contact era, the fur trade era, and the reserve era. — Chief Joseph, Nez Percé

The Nez Percé were a semi-nomadic Sahaptian-speaking tribe of American Indians who lived in the inland Northwest long before the arrival of the Europeans. The tribe's name means "Pierced ears," possibly referring to the practice of gauging the ears of young males with beads or other objects. The Nez Percé were the southernmost tribe of the Northern Shoshonean cultural area, and were probably the most numerous of the Shoshonean tribes. At the time of contact with the Europeans, the Nez Percé population was estimated at 10,000 to 15,000.
The Nez Percé were skilled hunters who moved from place to place in search of game. They followed the seasonal migrations of the buffalo, which provided them with both food and raw materials. The tribe's economy was based on the buffalo. The Nez Percé did not plant crops or practice agriculture. They were also skilled traders, and often traveled great distances in search of trade goods.
The Nez Percé were a peaceful people. They did not have a concept of private property. They shared everything they had, and worked together to hunt, fish, and gather berries. When a family group or a band grew too large, the members would divide and go their separate ways. Sometimes a group would join another band, or a family would adopt a new member. In this way, the Nez Percé were constantly changing and growing.

The story is set in Paris and describes the relationships between three characters, a young American named Nick Adams, a French girl named Catherine, and a French veteran of World War I named André. The line also appears in the film version of the story, directed by Lasse Hallström and released in 1996.

Variant
One night two men came down the alley. One was dressed for business, the other for bed.

The story
This story is one of several tales told by Canadian Native Indians about the origin of smoking. In this version, the people lived a happy life until two cruel men from a neighboring tribe stole their women. The angry men went to the mountain, gathered some sacred fire, and blew it toward the intruders. The smoke was so hot that it burned the thieves' faces and legs, and they cried out in pain. The women were horrified by the sight and begged their husbands to stop. One man, however, laughed at their cries and said, "That's not hot enough. Let's make it hotter." He gathered more fire and blew it harder. This time the flames caught fire to the thieves' beards and mustaches. Still they did not give up. "That's still not hot enough," one of them sneered. "Let's go back and get more fire." But as they turned to leave, a great lightning bolt came down from the sky and struck them both, killing them instantly. From that time on, the people placed a great stone at the foot of the mountain as a memorial to the two brave men who had given their lives to protect their wives. And from that time on, smoking was a part of every ceremony, a reminder of the sacrifice made long ago.

The Meaning of the dream
This dream is about coming to terms with pain.  The two men represent aspects of yourself that you have forgotten or repressed. The dancing represents the release of energy that takes place when two of these aspects come together. The gun represents conflict or hurt. The dance away represents the avoiding of conflict or hiding of pain. The rock represents a solid foundation or a reality check. There is usually a lot of pain and grief underlying dreams of this nature.

Summary
A dream that involves dancing often represents a release of emotion or energy. The dream might be alerting you to an upcoming emotional storm or crisis. It could also indicate that you are suppressing or keeping emotions hidden. Look for the meaning behind the dance and the music. Who is dancing and with whom? What is surrounding the dance? Are there any conflicts or problems associated with the dream? It is important to pay attention to your emotions during the dream and after waking up. Try writing down your thoughts and feelings in a journal. This can help you gain insight and understand the dream better.

One potential interpretation
A man dancing with an aspect of himself represents a release of repressed emotion or energy. The blue jacket means he is expressing feelings that have been hidden or forgotten. The kiss represents resolution of conflict or pain. The rock symbolizes a reminder of reality or a foundation for new understanding.

The answer is: ...came down from the hills on Miners Ridge, near Egulac, British Columbia, to hunt beaver. They came upon a group of men from another tribe, from above Canoe Ridge, also out hunting. A fight started over some beaver meat. Wawathum, a prominent chief of the Egaulac, took off his dress of animal skins and tossed it aside. Then he seized a gun and began shooting at the rival tribal men. His friend fled. Wawathum was eventually captured and brought before the other tribal leaders. They decided to execute him for fighting and, as was their custom, they tied him to a tree and sealed his mouth with glue. Over two hundred tribesmen helped drag the tree where he was tied to the edge of the cliff near present-day Heredosome, British Columbia.The execution was part of a wide-ranging feud between the Tribal Union and the alliance of coastal tribes known as the Shuswap, over trading rights with the newly arrived Spanish and English traders. The feud was to last forty years and would end with the demise of the Tribal Union as a separate entity.

But as the brothers were eating, one of them noticed that a bowl of soup was empty. He filled it with snow from the nearby mountain. When the people of the village saw this, they became angry. How dare these outsiders pollute their feast?

Before there could be any trouble, however, the two brothers had disappeared. They had heard a noise in the forest and had gone to investigate. When they returned, they had a message. A great army was coming. The people of the village needed their help.

And so the two brothers led the people of the village against the enemy. And in the end, the people of the village won. But the two brothers had disappeared again. This time they had gone to the forest to live. And that is where they stayed, living off the land and helping those in need, for the rest of their days.

This story is from the Salish people. It is a story of hospitality and of helping others. It reminds us that sometimes outsiders can bring us trouble, but sometimes they can bring us help. And it reminds us that we must be open to both.

This story is a part of the Métis storytelling tradition. It was told by John Pocosang, a Métis storyteller, to Frances Bernier in 1966. The story is a part of the Indigenous storytelling tradition of the Plains Cree, Saulteaux, and Métis peoples. In this story, the people dance around a bonfire on the banks of the Saskatchewan River. This type of dance is called the Fancy Dance. It was created by the Métis people in the early 19th century. The dance is a combination of the European waltz and the Indigenous Pow Wow dance. It was originally performed as a competition between groups of dancers. The dancers wear fancy costumes and perform intricate steps. The dance has been popular among the Métis people for over 200 years. It is still performed at Pow Wows and cultural festivals.

According to the tale, recorded by early ethnologists, two men from the Egulac band of the Sinixt were out in the woods one night when they heard the sounds of singing and laughter approaching. Thinking that this was a group of women coming to steal their berries and roots, the two men prepared to defend their supplies. But when they saw that it was actually three women dancing merrily towards them, they joined in the celebration, and soon many more people arrived, including more women and children, as well as additional men from other bands.

Jingle Dress Dance is a dance of the Ojibwe people. It originated as a type of harvest or search dance, but was later suppressed by Christian missionaries. Much of what is known about the earliest history of the dance comes from stories told by elderly Ojibwe people in the mid-20th century.

History
The Jingle Dress Dance was developing as a distinct dance form at least a century before the arrival of the Europeans in North America. Some Native American historians believe that the dance came from the southeastern woodlands. The dance spread westward as the population of the eastern woodlands continued to grow. According to one legend, the dance was introduced to the northwestern plains at a time when the tribes were suffering from smallpox. A healer named Clear Sky was credited with bringing the dance to the Cheyenne people. He told the Cheyenne that the dance would bring rain in the spring and that their people would be healed if they danced it properly.

EuropeanContact with Europeans caused a significant change in the way the dance was performed. missionaries brought fiddle playing and square dance styles from England and France. These influenced the music and dance style of the Jingle Dress Dance as it is currently performed. The dance became less flexible and more rhythmic as the people began to dance to the beat of the drums rather than singing the music as they had before.

Role of the dance in Native American culture
The Jingle Dress Dance is an integral part of Native American culture. The dance tells the story of the harvest, or gives thanks

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to fish where they knew a great number of fish were. They had a very good fire going and were enjoying themselves suddenly a crazy thought came to one of them that maybe the fire would burn the fish so they both jumped up and started to run back to the canoes as fast as they could.

One of the men fell into the river and nearly drowned before they finally got back to the canoes and pushed off to paddle back to Egulac. 

The crazy thought that almost cost them their lives was because Egulac was a village situated near the mouth of the river. It was well known that any fire on the river would attract hordes of fish. The two young men thought that the fire would chase the fish away. They didn't know that fish have no concept of fire, or of danger. They simply respond to stimuli. The men were lucky that they didn't drown or get dragged under by a panicking fish.

As a moral to the story, we can assume that the two young men learned a lesson that day. That lesson being, that fires on the river don't scare fish, they attract them.

// Twomen of Egulac //

egulac – orOne night two men from Egulac– is a First Nation community located on the south shore of Lillooet Lake in the province of British Columbia, Canada. The community is within the traditional territory of the Tzinququa' Robin Hood. The community is named after the Tzinququa' Robin Hood, a supernatural being who protected the area's original inhabitants from the invasion of the Lillooet band of the Kwakwaka'wio' wald. The community is now home to a provincial park and a youth camp, as well as a couple of private residences. There is also a First Nation bureau and a band office.

The story of the Twomen of Egulac is a common theme among the narratives of the supernatural beings who protect and govern the natural world. In the story, two brave men from Egulac went on a hunting expedition deep into the forest. As was their custom, they sang their ancestral songs as they travelled. Suddenly, they heard a chant coming from nearby. It was the voice of the Twomen, who were questioning whether the men were really from Egulac. The men sang back their ancestral songs, and the Twomen were impressed. They welcomed the men into their camp and fed them. But as the men were leaving, they saw that their dogs had eaten all the Twomen's dogs. The angry Twomen chased the men back to Egulac, but the men used their ancestral songs to hide at a river. The Twomen could not catch them, but they cursed the men, saying that they would never be effective hunters again. It is a traditional story of the Tlingit people. This story is sometimes told when someone is born out of wedlock and is meant to instruct them on the proper way to get married and maintain a healthy marriage. The story is told as a conversation between two men, One Man and Tall Man, although other versions may have more or fewer characters.

One Man and Tall Man were good friends and they spent a great deal of their time together. One Man lived in a very small house with his wife and children. Although One Man worked very hard, his family was always cold and hungry. Tall Man, on the other hand, lived in a very big house with many rooms. Tall Man's wife prepared delicious meals and his children played happily. One Man was very jealous of Tall Man and his good fortune.
One day One Man said to Tall Man, "Why are your wife and children always so happy? How do you live in such a big house and feed all of us so well?"
Tall Man looked at One Man with a kind smile and said, "It is very simple. I go to the potlatch and give away everything I have and more. I dance the dance of happiness and all the people love me. Your daughters would marry any man they choose and your sons would become great leaders. Your family would be happy and content."
One Man thought about what Tall Man had said and realized that he had never given anything away. He decided to attend a potlatch and give away everything he had. He even gaveaway his wife and children. The people were amazed at One Man's generosity and gifted him even more in return. One Man left the potlatch with a happy heart, knowing that his family would be happy and content. From then on, One Man became known as the most generous man in Egulac.

Egulac is a mountain in the Yukon Territory, Canada, located in the north of Watson Lake National Park. It is 70 kilometres (43 mi) northeast of Whitehorse. The name is from the Tanana language, and means "mountain of the red earth". It is 763 metres (2,500 ft) high.

The story
In the story, the two men from Egulac come down from the mountain and walk along the frost-covered river bank, making no sound. They come across a small village, where they are surprised to find people still asleep. One of the men had a dream, in which a great army marched from the south to destroy the northern villages. The people of the village welcome the men as friends and heroes, but the two strangers leave at dawn, walking back up the mountain. They did not want to be seen by the people who were sleeping.

Analysis
The story exemplifies the theme of the supernatural in Native American literature. The two men are mysterious figures who seem to have powers beyond the normal human span. They are associated with the mountain, and may be guardians of the natural world. The dream sequence in the story foreshadows the coming of destruction, perhaps from the white settlers. The story can be seen as a cautionary tale about the dangers of sleeping through the arrival of strangers.

Origins
The story may be based on an actual dream reported by Dena'ina elder William Wood Sr. to anthropologist John R. Swanton. It was first published in Swanton's 1932 book The Tlingit.

This is a story from the Ojibwe people's creation myth. What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: Egulac was a violent spirit who lived in the spring water. It terrorized the people, killing them and destroying their properties. The two men were actually servants of Egulac. They were sent to bring back the spirit when he became angry. But the servants had stolen some of the sacred cattle of Ogikii, the chief of the cattle, and brought them along instead. Ogikii had given the servants the power to change into different animals, including cattle. The two men had changed into cattle when they stole the animals. Now they had changed back into men.

Other versions
In another version of the story, the two men are not servants of Egulac. They are hunters who have offended the spirit of the forest. They are punished by being turned into cattle. Eventually, they are changed back into men after promising to behave better.

In another version, the two men are actually the children of the hero, Nanabozho. They are out looking for strawberries when they anger a giant by taking more than their share. The giant turns them into cattle. Later, Nanabozho goes to the forest to find his children and takes along a bag of tobacco to offer as a peace offering. The giant agrees to give back the children in exchange for the tobacco.

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals [wp="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/egulac"]Huntley, British Columbia ]. At about midnight they were returning home without having seen any game when they came across a camp near the mouth of Bonneau Cove.  Inside they discovered four armed men, two White andtwo First Nations men. The White men fled when they discovered the natives had seen them. But the native warriors gave pursuit.  The two young hunters hidden behind a tree, watched as eight kivas were built that night and two people were buried. When daylight came and the egulac people had left, the two young men went to the cove and saw human bones belonging to two people. The bones were laid to rest again that day, but the two young men vowed to return the next night and watch again. And so began the saga of the Egulac bone creek site [1]. The fossil bones were found in 1883, during a campaign of paleontological survey in Canadian deserts undertaken by the Geological Survey of Canada. A skeleton was found complete to the pelvis and was later named Dinotherium igloicruste. Later work by Harold Pulman and Robin McGregor suggest these bones are in fact from two separate individuals. One skeleton is partly on the bank of Bonneau Cove and the other is more complete skeleton is located four metres (13 ft) distant. Thebone creek site is a collection of fossilized animal bones that were deposited as floodplains or river channel deposits during the Cambrian period. The site is extremely important to paleontologists as it gives a reasonably complete evolutionary sequence of a number of families of animals. Of especial importance is the bone cemetery, where a series of flat, rounded bones bearing crenelations-scalloped margins-were found. These bones

One night two young men from Egulac went down to the river to hunt seals and while they were there it became foggy and calm. Then they heard war-cries, and they thought: "Maybe this is a war-party". They escaped to the shore, and hid behind a log. Now canoes came up, and they heard the noise of paddles, and saw one canoe coming up to them. There were five men in the canoe, and they said: "What do you think? We wish to take you along. We are going up the river to make war on the people." One of the young men said, "I have no arrows." "Arrows are in the canoe," they said. "I will not go along. I might be killed. My relatives do not know where I have gone. But you," he said, turning to the other, "may go with them." So one of the young men went, but the other returned home. And the warriors went on up the river to a town on the other side of Kalama. The people came down to the water and they began to fight, and many were killed. But presently the young man heard one of the warriors say, "Quick, let us go home: that man has been hit." Now he thought: "Oh, they are ghosts." He did not feel sick, but they said he had been shot. So the canoes went back to Egulac and the young man went ashore to his house and made a fire. And he told everybody and said: "Behold I accompanied the ghosts, and we went to fight. Many of our fellows were killed. Now quickly let us make a feast, for I have been with the dead."  So they made a feast that night. And he told them all the stories that the ghosts had told him. And he lived a long time after that.

The other young man jumped up and ran away as fast as he could. He went to the village and told what had happened. Then the people came together and made a canoe to go and bring back the bones of their relative. They set out on the journey and went up the river, and when they reached the place where the young man had been killed, they took his bones and put them in the canoe. Then they went back to the village and buried the bones. After that the people went out and made a war-party. They went up the river and made war on the people who had killed their relative. They made war on them until they took revenge for the death of their relative.

== Information == 
This story is from the Tlingit people. According to the information given in the story, it appears to take place in the region of Egulac, and involves two young men and some young women. The story does not make clear whether the young men and women are related, but mentions that they are from different clans. The story is a love story, and is possibly a kind of courtship story. The story does not have a clear beginning or ending, and is more like a series of events.

We have them!" When the young man heard this, he knew that it was a ghost war-party. He knew that if he did not escape, he would be killed. He left the canoe and swam to the shore, and as soon as he got to the forest he began to cry: "I have escaped! I have escaped!" He had heard that the ghosts were crying and waiting for those who were killed in battle. He went back to Egulac and told what had happened, and they were glad that he had come back. Eventually, he married the girl he loved, and they lived together nicely, because he had come back from the dead.

The message
The message from Glooscap was simple. If the people of the south wanted to live, they had to start living according to the way of the Red Man. Glooscap had seen the whites encroaching on their land, pushing them westwards. He had seen their cities. He had seen their weapons. He knew they were coming. But, he said, there was still time to change. The whites were like rushing rivers that ignored the smaller streams. But the smaller streams could join forces and divert the rivers. That was what Glooscap asked of the Red Men. They had the power, he said, to stop the whites from taking their land.

The response
The two messengers returned to the villages of the south. They told of the message from Glooscap. The people were terrified. The whites were indeed coming, pushing ever westwards. The villages were growing bigger, and the people were losing their land. But the message was clear. If they wanted to live, they had to change. They had to stop fighting among themselves. They had to learn to live in peace. And they had to learn to live in harmony with the land. Only then would the whites stop coming. Only then would they be able to hold on to their land.

It was an obscure term in a 17th-century French manuscript that baffled scholars until 1996, when translator Michael Neurauter discovered that it referred to the small Group of montagne pines (Pinusborealis) that can be found in the Egula sector of Banff National Park in Alberta, Canada. The term was later confirmed by Jacques Marquignault, a Forest Canada scientist, whose French-Language Quebec newspaper, Le Devoisie, had run a contest for a fitting name for the then recently discovered conific. Since that time, the common name mountable pine has been proposed as a preliminary common name as a reference to it having been formerly used as a translatable term for Larix laurentius ssp. betulifolia in French.

Description
The mounted pine is a matsis tree and is the least-known and most-recently described of the four subspecies of white pine native to Canada. It is the smallest subspecies of white pine found in North America, typically growing only to 10 m (33 ft) in height. Despite its small size, it is distinct from other white pines in having somewhat flatter, more horizontal branching; its green buds and very short, thin needles (only 5–7 mm (2.0–2.7 in) long) set it apart from other white pines. Its crown is relatively close to the ground and becomes more flat-topped with age.

Habitat
The subspecies is endemic to the tall forests of the interior of British Columbia and Alberta, in the west of the Canadian Cordillera. It is confined to a restricted area of the mountains of south-west British Columbia and east of Banff National Park in Alberta. The population trend is thought to be stable, although fires and rising temperatures are thought to pose future threats to the species.

Name
The name mountable pine

The answer is: ...came down from the mountain in British Columbia carrying a freshly cut bamboo pole. They planted it in the ground at a certain spot and then spent the night at nearby Regina Camp. The next day they left without returning to Egulac. Nobody knows where they came from or who they were. The bamboo pole is still there. It is said that: "If anybody goes to that spot and touches the pole, he will be possessed by the devil."

The location
Regina Camp is on the north shore of Lillooet Lake, which is on the boundary between the provinces of British Columbia and Alberta in western Canada. The area is surrounded by mountains.

Further information
This story is told in the book Fifth Generation: Conscious Elders Speak, by Charles C. Managan. The book is based on tape-recorded interviews with Native American elders. The story is attributed to "two old-time Ktunaxa Indians."

The details of the story
A young man from Egulac went off to the city for higher education. While he was away, two young men from the Egulac reserve on the north shore of Whitefish Lake went down to the mouth of the river to get some firewood for the chief. While they were away, two middle-aged men from the reserve threatened to burn down the young man's house if he didn't give them his allowance. The two young men went back to the city and told their friend what had happened. The young man was very upset and wanted to go home right away. But his friends told him to stay, finish his education, and take over the family business when he graduated.

Variants
One version of the story has it that the two young men came across a giant beast in the forest and sought refuge at the chief's house. Another version says that the two young men were accused of theft and sought shelter at the chief's house. In both versions, the young men were advised to leave and return when they were older.

Appearance
The narrator of the story, Crazy Bear, is depicted as a wise old man, although the illustrator adds a touch of madness to his appearance. The men from the city are dressed in suits, with one wearing atop hat. The two young men seek refuge at the chief's house because they have broken a taboo.

Artist's approach
The artist began by researching the social structure of the group that would become the Paddle People. He concluded that they were a matrilineal society with a chief and council. He realized that since this was non-Indigenous land, the traditional ways of the native people had been disrupted. He decided to capture the sense of dislocation and trauma that comes from losing one's land
